pairs.en: On the same day, the third of the month, we remember our holy fathers DALMATOS, FAUSTOS and ISAKIOS — the last name also written Isaakios.
*Three men circle your throne on high, Most High: Faustos, Isakios, Dalmatos.* *On the third of the month Dalmatos died, and Isakios, and Faustos too.*

Of these three saints, Dalmatos was a soldier in the Second Company of the imperial guard, in the reign of the emperor Theodosius the Great, in the year 368 — and he lived devoutly, in a way that pleased God. Later he left behind his wife, his children and everything the world had to offer. He took with him only his son Faustos, went to Saint Isakios, became a monk there, and rose to the very greatest heights of holiness.

This remarkable Isakios had gone to live in the desert, in silence and stillness, from his early youth, and he practised every kind of virtue. That is why his words carried such weight: they were backed by the life he lived.

Now the emperor Valens was an Arian — he denied that Christ is fully God — and when he marched out to make war on the Scythians and the Goths, Isakios came up to him and said: “Open the churches to the Orthodox, your majesty, and you will win your war.”
The emperor would not listen. He lost his temper and said to the holy man: “When I get back from the war, you will be punished for those words of yours.”

The holy man answered: “If you come back from this war at all, then the Lord God never spoke to me. You will fight your battle — but you will run from your enemies, and you will be burned alive.” And that is exactly what happened. He was shut inside a barn, and there he was burned to death.

When the time came for Isakios to depart to the Lord, he appointed Dalmatos as abbot of the monastery. Saint Atticus was patriarch of Constantinople at the time. Dalmatos then distinguished himself in the ascetic life: he once went forty days without food, and for another forty days he was caught up out of himself in prayer.

So he came to be honoured and revered — by the emperors, by the senate, and by the holy fathers who gathered at Ephesus for the Third Ecumenical Council in the year 431. Those fathers voted him archimandrite, the senior abbot over other abbots, and they ruled that his successors after him should hold permanent authority over his monastery.

Having distinguished himself in all this, the man whose memory we sing departed to the Lord and was laid to rest in his own monastery. (Note that the Greek life of these holy fathers survives in the Great Lavra on Mount Athos; it begins: “This great and wonderful Isaakios.”)

sections.heading: Saint Stephen the Priest-Martyr, Pope of Rome

pairs.en: On the same day we remember the holy priest-martyr STEPHEN, Pope of Rome, and those who suffered with him.
*Stephen was beheaded, and seized a crown from heaven —* *a pope before, and now a great martyr as well.*

He lived in the reigns of the emperors Decius, Valerian and Gallienus, around the year 250. Because Christians were being hunted down, he stayed in hiding in Rome. He taught the pagans who came to him, instructed them in the faith of Christ and baptised them; and from among them he ordained priests, deacons and readers. Some of these men were arrested, confessed Christ, and won the martyr's crown — because he had given them the courage for it.

For that reason the blessed man gave himself up to the governor. He was taken to the temple of Ares, the war-god, and there he prayed — and the whole temple shook, and part of it came crashing down. The soldiers took fright and ran.
The saint then withdrew and went to the tomb of Lucia the martyr, in Campania in southern Italy, and there he went on celebrating the Liturgy — the bloodless offering.

Later the soldiers came looking for him and found him, and when they had found him they tortured him at length, and at last beheaded him. So this man of blessed memory received a double crown — the crown his own name means — as a bishop, and as one of the Lord's champions.
(Note that the Greek account of this Saint Stephen's martyrdom survives in the Great Lavra on Mount Athos; it begins: “In the times of Valerian and Gallienus.”)
We remember our holy father and confessor JOHN, abbot of the Monastery of Pataleria.
*Blessed John — true to the meaning of your name,* *you proved a house worthy of God's grace.*
Saint SALOME the Myrrh-bearer, who died in peace.
*Her body rolled away from her like the stone from the tomb —* *and now Salome sees Christ himself, not the grave of Christ.*
Saint THEOCLITO the Wonderworker, who died in peace.
*Theoclito proves her name true by the way she lived —* *“called by God,” and shown to be called when she put off the body.*

This holy woman Theoclito lived in the reign of the emperor Theophilos — the emperor who hated Christ and made war on the holy icons — around the year 829. She came from the district known as the Optimatoi, in what is now north-west Turkey, across the water from Constantinople. Her parents were named Constantine and Anastasia. She was brought up from her earliest years in a way that pleased God, and she kept a careful watch over herself. Later her parents pressed her into marriage, but the husband they chose turned out to be as good-hearted as she was; his name was Zacharias.

Once she was married, this blessed woman gave away charity beyond counting. Above all she gave herself to reading and studying the holy Scriptures — and she did not only read them, she completed her reading by doing it, taking up every good thing and every virtue she found there.

She worked with her hands all day long, and served whatever the poor needed — every poor person who came to her house. On top of that she waited on her own household staff as well, because she was so deeply humble.

When the time came for her to depart to the Lord, this woman of blessed memory called all her friends together and told them in advance that she would die on a particular day. And it turned out exactly as she had said.

We cannot describe all the miracles that happened after ⟨…⟩ her holy remains were laid to rest — we are keeping this short. But there is one we have to tell, and even if we wanted to stay silent about it we could not, because it is too great a thing to pass over.

This saint's relatives have a custom of lifting up her thrice-holy and most honoured body once a year. It is whole and undecayed. They change her clothes for fresh ones; they smooth down the hair of her head, which is white; then they cut the nails of her hands and her feet, exactly as if she were alive. After that they chant the Trisagion, and so they lay her body back in its casket.
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.

It appears that the monastery itself took its name from this same holy Dalmatos — “the Monastery of the Dalmatoi,” as it is called in the entry for the thirtieth of May, the day on which Saint Isakios is commemorated on his own.
*The date is wrong: Theodosius came to the throne in 379.* — the 1868 editor
*Decius was succeeded in 251 by Gallus; and when Gallus too had been killed, Valerian came to the throne in 253 together with his son Gallienus.* — the 1868 editor
This Saint Lucia is commemorated on the sixth of July.
